subject: Humanities
title: Geography: Our Environment (Class 7)
sub: NCERT Class 7 Geography, chapters 1–9 · practising the IGCSE way
strategyIntro: Geography marks go to correct terms, real examples and clear reasons. Close the book, answer from memory, then check.

strategy.title: Short answers
points: Add a named example where you can (Bhuj 2001, the Sahara, the Deccan plateau).

strategy.title: Give reasons / Explain
points: Say what happens, then why, with 'because' or 'so'.
The marks tell you how many points to make.

strategy.title: Describe and compare
points: Describe: where, what it is like, examples.
Compare: say what is the same, then what is different, using numbers.

commandWords: Say what something is like, with details and examples.
Say what is similar and what is different.
quizIntro: Pick one or more chapters above, then answer. Each answer shows why it's right.

flashIntro: Pick one or more chapters above. Answer out loud, then flip. 'Not yet' cards come back sooner.

flashcards.back: The place, people, things and nature that surround any living organism: a mix of natural and human-made.
Biotic: the living world (plants, animals). Abiotic: the non-living world (land, water, air).
The solid crust or hard top layer of the Earth, made of rocks and minerals and covered by soil.
The domain of water: rivers, lakes, seas, oceans.
The thin layer of air around the Earth, held by gravity. It protects us from harmful rays and heat.
The narrow zone where land, water and air interact to support life: plants and animals.
The relationship between living organisms, and between organisms and their surroundings. E.g. a pond, forest, desert.

flashcards.front: Give four examples of the human-made environment.
flashcards.back: Buildings, roads, bridges, parks, industries, monuments (any four).

flashcards.front: Where does the word 'environment' come from?
flashcards.back: The French 'environner', meaning neighbourhood.

flashcards.front: Name the three layers of the Earth.
flashcards.back: Crust, mantle, core.

flashcards.front: Why is the continental crust called sial?
flashcards.back: It is mainly silica (si) and alumina (al).

flashcards.front: Why is the oceanic crust called sima?
flashcards.back: It is mainly silica (si) and magnesium (ma).
About 35 km on continents and only 5 km on the ocean floors. It is the thinnest layer.

flashcards.front: What is the core made of, and what is it called?
flashcards.back: Nickel and iron: nife (ni + fe).

flashcards.front: How are extrusive igneous rocks formed? Example?
flashcards.back: Lava cools quickly on the surface; fine-grained. Basalt (the Deccan plateau).

flashcards.front: How are intrusive igneous rocks formed? Example?
flashcards.back: Magma cools slowly deep inside the crust; large grains. Granite.
Small pieces of rock are carried, deposited and pressed into layers. They may contain fossils.
Rocks changed by heat and pressure: clay → slate, limestone → marble.
Rocks changing from one type to another in a cycle: igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma → igneous.
A naturally occurring substance with definite physical properties and chemical composition.
Because of the circular movement of molten magma inside the Earth. They move a few millimetres each year.
Endogenic act inside the Earth (earthquakes, volcanoes). Exogenic act on the surface (rivers, wind, glaciers, sea waves).
A vent in the Earth's crust through which molten material erupts suddenly.
Focus: where the earthquake starts in the crust. Epicentre: the place on the surface directly above it.
With a seismograph; its magnitude on the Richter scale.
Weathering: rocks breaking up on the surface. Erosion: the wearing away of land by water, wind and ice.
A lake formed when a meander loop is cut off from the river.
When a river floods, it deposits fine soil (sediments) on its banks, making flat fertile land.
Near the sea the river splits into distributaries and drops its load; the sediments from all the mouths form a delta.

flashcards.front: Sea cave → sea arch → stack: how?
flashcards.back: Waves widen cracks into caves; caves become arches; the roof falls leaving wall-like stacks.
Rocks, sand and silt deposited by a glacier.
Wind erodes the lower part of a rock more than the top, leaving a narrow base and wide top.
Very fine sand carried far by wind and deposited over large areas (e.g. China).

flashcards.front: Which two gases make up most of the air?
flashcards.back: Nitrogen (78%) and oxygen (21%).
Bacteria in the soil and roots take nitrogen from the air and change it so plants can use it.
Carbon dioxide traps heat radiated from the Earth, keeping it warm enough to live on.
Extra carbon dioxide (factory smoke, car fumes) traps more heat and raises Earth's temperature, melting ice and raising sea levels.

flashcards.front: Name the five layers of the atmosphere in order.
flashcards.back: Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere.

flashcards.front: Why is the troposphere the most important layer?
flashcards.back: We breathe its air, and almost all weather happens there. Average height 13 km.

flashcards.front: Why is the stratosphere good for flying planes?
flashcards.back: It is almost free of clouds and weather. It also has the ozone layer.

flashcards.front: What happens in the mesosphere? The thermosphere?
flashcards.back: Meteorites burn up in the mesosphere. The ionosphere in the thermosphere reflects radio waves.
Weather: hour-to-hour, day-to-day condition of the atmosphere. Climate: the average weather over a long time.
Incoming solar energy received by the Earth. It decreases from the equator to the poles.

flashcards.front: How does air pressure change with height?
flashcards.back: It is highest at sea level and falls as you go up.
Permanent (trade winds, westerlies, easterlies), seasonal (monsoons), local (land and sea breeze, loo).
Convectional, orographic (relief) and cyclonic.
The moisture (water vapour) in the air.
The process by which water keeps changing form and circulating between oceans, atmosphere and land.

flashcards.front: How much of Earth's water is in the oceans?
flashcards.back: About 97.3%. Ice caps hold about 2%; very little is usable fresh water.
The amount of salt in grams in 1000 grams of water. Average ocean salinity: 35 parts per thousand.

flashcards.front: Why can swimmers float in the Dead Sea?
flashcards.back: Its very high salt content (340 g per litre) makes the water dense.
22 March.
By wind scraping across the ocean surface; stronger wind, bigger waves.
A huge 'harbour wave' caused by an earthquake, volcano or underwater landslide (e.g. Indian Ocean, 26 Dec 2004).
The gravitational pull of the Moon (and Sun) on the Earth's water.
Spring tides: highest, at full and new moon (Sun, Moon, Earth in a line). Neap tides: low, at the first and last quarter.
They help ships reach harbour, bring fish closer to shore, and can make electricity.
Streams of water moving along definite paths. Warm currents start near the equator; cold ones near the poles.

flashcards.front: What happens where warm and cold currents meet?
flashcards.back: Good fishing grounds (e.g. around Japan), but fog that makes navigation difficult.

flashcards.front: Which two factors mainly decide vegetation?
flashcards.back: Temperature and moisture (also slope and thickness of soil).

flashcards.front: Three broad kinds of natural vegetation?
flashcards.back: Forests, grasslands and shrubs.

flashcards.front: Where are tropical evergreen forests found? Trees?
flashcards.back: Near the equator; heavy rain all year. Hardwoods like rosewood, ebony, mahogany.

flashcards.front: Why are tropical deciduous forests called monsoon forests?
flashcards.back: They are in monsoon regions (much of India); trees shed leaves in the dry season to save water. Sal, teak, neem, shisham.

flashcards.front: Where are temperate evergreen forests found?
flashcards.back: Mid-latitude coasts on eastern margins (south-east USA, south China, south-east Brazil). Oak, pine, eucalyptus.

flashcards.front: Why are Mediterranean regions called 'orchards of the world'?
flashcards.back: Hot dry summers and mild rainy winters suit citrus fruits, figs, olives and grapes.
Tall softwood evergreens at 50°–70°N and high altitudes. Used for pulp, paper, matchboxes. Chir, pine, cedar.
Savanna (East Africa), campos (Brazil), llanos (Venezuela).
Pampas (Argentina), prairie (N. America), veld (S. Africa), steppe (C. Asia), downs (Australia).
Mosses, lichens and tiny shrubs in polar regions; animals have thick fur (seals, walruses, polar bears).
A place where people build their homes.
Temporary: occupied for a short time (forests, deserts, mountains). Permanent: homes built to stay.
Seasonal movement of herders in search of new pastures.
Compact: houses built close together. Scattered: houses spread out.

flashcards.front: Why did early settlements grow near rivers?
flashcards.back: Water was available and the land was fertile.
Roadways, railways, waterways, airways.
Metalled = pucca; unmetalled = kutcha.
They carry heavy goods and people over long distances quickly and cheaply.

flashcards.front: Which transport is cheapest for heavy, bulky goods?
flashcards.back: Waterways.

flashcards.front: What are the drawbacks of airways?
flashcards.back: Most expensive (fuel costs) and affected by bad weather like fog and storms.
Highways connecting Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.
The Trans-Siberian Railway, from St Petersburg to Vladivostok.
Newspapers, radio and television, which communicate with many people at once.
South America, on the equator (10°N–10°S); the largest river basin in the world.
Hot and wet all year; rain almost every day; very humid day and night.

flashcards.front: Why is the rainforest floor dark?
flashcards.back: The thick 'roof' of leaves and branches stops sunlight reaching the ground.

flashcards.front: Name birds and animals of the Amazon rainforest.
flashcards.back: Toucans, humming birds; monkeys, sloths, tapirs; anaconda, boa constrictor; piranha fish.
Clearing land by cutting and burning trees, growing crops until the soil is used up, then moving to a new plot.

flashcards.front: Staple food of the Amazon people?
flashcards.back: Manioc (cassava). They also grow tapioca, pineapple, sweet potato.
A large apartment-like house with a steeply slanting roof.
The Trans-Amazon highway (1970) opened up the forest, leading to deforestation and loss of tribal ways of life.

flashcards.front: Climate and crops of the Ganga–Brahmaputra basin?
flashcards.back: Monsoon climate (mid-June to mid-September). Paddy (main crop), wheat, maize, jute, sugarcane; tea on slopes.
Elephants, tigers, one-horned rhino (Brahmaputra plain), Bengal tiger and crocodiles (delta), susu dolphin.

flashcards.front: What does the susu (blind dolphin) tell us?
flashcards.back: Its presence shows the river is healthy; pollution is killing it.

flashcards.front: Name big cities on the Ganga.
flashcards.back: Allahabad, Kanpur, Varanasi, Lucknow, Patna, Kolkata.
Both have low rainfall and scanty vegetation. Hot: e.g. the Sahara. Cold: e.g. Ladakh.
The world's largest desert: about 8.54 million sq km, touching 11 countries in North Africa.
Scorching hot days (up to 50°C; record 57.7°C at Al Azizia, Libya), cold nights near 0°C, short rainy season.
A green island around water in the desert, with date palms.

flashcards.front: Plants and animals of the Sahara?
flashcards.back: Cactus, date palms, acacia; camels, hyenas, jackals, foxes, scorpions, snakes, lizards.

flashcards.front: Who are the Bedouins and Tuaregs?
flashcards.back: Nomadic tribes of the Sahara who rear goats, sheep, camels and horses.

flashcards.front: Why do people in the Sahara wear heavy robes?
flashcards.back: To protect themselves from dust storms and hot winds.
Oil in Algeria, Libya and Egypt; office buildings and highways; trucks replacing camels; Tuaregs working as tourist guides.
'La' = mountain pass, 'Dak' = country.
Extremely cold and dry; below –40°C in winter; in the rain shadow of the Himalayas, under 10 cm of rain a year.
Grasses, shrubs, willows, poplars, apricots, apples, walnuts; yaks, wild goats and sheep; robins, raven, hoopoe.
Hemis, Thiksey, Shey, Lamayuru.
One of the coldest inhabited places on Earth.

examIntro: Write your answer first, then compare with the model. Check you used the right terms and gave reasons.

exam.q: Give reasons: why do humans modify their environment?
model: Human needs have grown and become more varied over time.
To meet them, people grow crops, build houses, roads and factories, and use more resources, which changes the natural surroundings.
exam.why: Need, then the action that follows from it.

exam.q: Describe the four domains of the environment.
model: The lithosphere is the solid crust of rocks and minerals, with soil and landforms like mountains and plains.
The hydrosphere is all the water: rivers, lakes, seas and oceans.
The atmosphere is the thin layer of air around the Earth that protects us from the sun's harmful rays.
The biosphere is the narrow zone where land, water and air meet to support plants and animals.
exam.why: One clear sentence for each domain.

exam.q: Explain how extrusive and intrusive igneous rocks are formed.
model: Both form when molten magma cools and becomes solid.
Extrusive rocks form when lava comes out onto the surface and cools quickly, so they have very fine grains. Basalt, which makes up the Deccan plateau, is an example.
Intrusive rocks form when magma cools slowly deep inside the crust, so they have large grains. Granite is an example.
exam.why: Where it cools, how fast, the grain size, and an example for each.

model: Molten magma cools and becomes igneous rock.
Igneous rocks break into small particles that are carried, deposited and pressed into sedimentary rocks.
Heat and pressure change igneous and sedimentary rocks into metamorphic rocks, which can melt back into magma, so the cycle starts again.
exam.why: The stages in order, using the three rock names.

exam.q: Explain how an ox-bow lake is formed.
model: As a river enters the plain it twists and turns, forming large bends called meanders.
Continuous erosion and deposition along the sides bring the ends of a meander loop closer and closer.
In time the loop is cut off from the river, forming an ox-bow (cut-off) lake.
exam.why: Three steps in order with the key terms.

exam.q: Give reasons: why do buildings collapse during earthquakes?
model: When lithospheric plates move, the Earth's surface vibrates in waves that travel out from the epicentre.
These strong vibrations shake buildings, and weak structures crack and collapse, especially near the epicentre (e.g. Bhuj, 2001).
exam.why: Cause of the shaking, then its effect on buildings.

exam.q: Give reasons: why do wet clothes take longer to dry on a humid day?
model: On a humid day the air is already full of water vapour.
So it cannot take in much more moisture, and the water in the clothes evaporates slowly.

exam.q: Explain the greenhouse effect and how it leads to global warming.
model: Carbon dioxide in the atmosphere traps some of the heat radiated from the Earth. This greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm enough to live on.
Burning coal and oil, factory smoke and car fumes add more carbon dioxide, so more heat is trapped and the Earth's temperature rises: global warming.
This melts snow and ice in the coldest regions, so sea levels rise and coastal areas flood, and it may change climates and wipe out some plants and animals.
exam.why: The effect, its cause, and its consequences, in that order.

exam.q: What are tides and how are they caused?
model: Tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of ocean water, twice a day.
They are caused by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on the Earth's water; the water nearest the Moon is pulled up into a high tide.
At full and new moon the Sun, Moon and Earth are in a line, giving the highest (spring) tides; at the quarter moons they pull at an angle, giving low (neap) tides.
exam.why: Definition, cause, then the two kinds of tide.

exam.q: Give reasons: why do so many countries face water shortages when most of the Earth is covered by water?
model: About 97% of the Earth's water is salty ocean water and about 2% is frozen in ice caps.
Only a tiny fraction is fresh water in rivers, lakes and underground that people can use, and it is being polluted.
exam.why: Use the numbers from the distribution table.

model: They are the monsoon forests found in much of India, northern Australia and Central America.
The trees shed their leaves in the dry season to conserve water.
They have hardwoods like sal, teak, neem and shisham, and animals such as tigers, elephants and langurs.
exam.why: Where, a key feature, and examples of trees and animals.

exam.q: Explain why Mediterranean trees can survive dry summers.
model: Mediterranean regions have hot, dry summers.
The trees have thick bark and wax-coated leaves, which reduce water loss (transpiration).

exam.q: Compare the advantages and disadvantages of airways and waterways.
model: Airways are the fastest way to travel and can reach remote areas with no roads or railways; helicopters help in disasters.
But airways are the most expensive, because of fuel costs, and are affected by fog and storms.
Waterways are the cheapest way to carry heavy and bulky goods over long distances, using rivers, lakes and sea routes.
But they are slow and can only go where there is navigable water and ports.
exam.why: Advantages and disadvantages for both, with specific details.

exam.q: Explain why the population is dense in the plains of the Ganga–Brahmaputra basin but thin in the mountains.
model: The plains have flat land and fertile soil, so farming (especially paddy) is easy and supports many people.
The mountains have steep slopes and difficult terrain, so it is hard to farm and build.
So most people live on the plains and few live in the mountains.
exam.why: Compare both areas and give the reason for each.

exam.q: Describe how life in the Amazon basin is changing.
model: In the past the heart of the forest could only be reached by river.
The Trans-Amazon highway (1970) made all parts accessible, and forests are being cut down for land and wood.
This is destroying the rainforest and changing the traditional way of life of its people.
exam.why: Before, the change, and its effects.

exam.q: Give reasons: why is there scanty vegetation in deserts?
model: Deserts get very little rainfall, and in hot deserts the moisture evaporates faster than it collects.
Extreme temperatures (scorching heat, or freezing cold in cold deserts) also make it hard for plants to grow.

exam.q: Compare the climate of the Sahara and Ladakh.
model: Both are deserts with very low rainfall and scanty vegetation.
The Sahara is a hot desert: days can reach 50°C, but nights may be near 0°C.
Ladakh is a cold desert high in the Himalayas: winter temperatures fall below –40°C and summer days are only just above 0°C.
Ladakh gets under 10 cm of rain because it lies in the rain shadow of the Himalayas.
exam.why: A similarity, then the differences with numbers.
